problem: The claim that a fixed-point velocity record shows "flat (steady) or fluctuating (turbulent)" undoes the chapter's own correct distinction in Section 3 that laminar/steady and turbulent/unsteady are separate questions. A turbulent flow that is steady in the mean gives a fluctuating record with a constant mean, so 'fluctuating' alone does not mean turbulent, and a fluctuating record with a drifting mean means unsteady, not turbulent.
fix: Say: the probe shows whether the record is flat (steady), fluctuates about a constant mean (steady in the mean, as in turbulent flow), or drifts with time (unsteady). The size and randomness of the fluctuations, not their mere presence, is what marks turbulence.

problem: The question asks for all four labels, but the answer for the surge gives only unsteady, non-uniform and three-dimensional, plus 'rapidly varied', which is not one of the four labels. The order label (laminar or turbulent) is missing for the surge itself, so a 5-mark answer would lose marks.
fix: Add: the surge is also turbulent (random eddies and strong mixing); so the four labels are unsteady, non-uniform, turbulent and three-dimensional near the gate, with 'rapidly varied' added as the open-channel description of how fast conditions change in space and time.

problem: 'Open channels add one more label, rapidly varied unsteady flow' treats a compound of two independent axes as a single label. Rapidly varied flow is normally a sub-class of non-uniform flow and can be steady (a hydraulic jump on a steady flow); only a surge or bore is both rapidly varied and unsteady.
fix: Say: open-channel flow uses the same tests and adds gradually varied and rapidly varied as sub-classes of non-uniform flow; a surge or bore is the case that is both rapidly varied and unsteady.
